blocks.x: STAT 153 · Statistical Methods · Topic 4

"The only two sure things are death and taxes" — everything else in life, from whether you carry an umbrella to whether a patient's test result is a true positive, is governed at least in part by chance. Probability is the mathematical language for that chance, and it is the foundation on which all of inferential statistics is built.

By the end of this module, you will be able to…

items: 1Define probability, experiments, sample spaces and events, distinguish deterministic from random experiments, and construct sample spaces for simple and compound experiments (coin tosses, dice, family composition).
2State and apply the axioms of probability (Kolmogorov's axioms), and use the addition rule — including the special case of mutually exclusive events — to find P(A ∪ B).
3Apply the multiplication law of probability to compound events, and recognise and use the condition for independence, P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B).

4Compute conditional probabilities, apply the Total Probability Rule to break a complex event into a partition, and apply Bayes' Rule to "invert" conditional probabilities — the backbone of interpreting diagnostic test results (sensitivity, specificity, predictive values).

5Apply permutation and combination formulas to count ordered arrangements and unordered selections, and combine counting techniques with the classical definition of probability to solve compound-event problems.

blocks.x: Key definitions

Probability A measure of the likelihood of a random phenomenon or chance behaviour. Probability describes the long-term proportion with which a certain outcome will occur in situations involving short-term uncertainty. A probability close to 1 means high likelihood; close to 0 means low likelihood.

Random experiment Any process that generates a set of data or well-defined outcomes, whose result cannot be predicted with certainty — from tossing a coin to screening 50 people for a disease. This contrasts with a deterministic experiment, whose result is not subject to chance.

Sample space (S) and event The sample space is the collection of all possible outcomes of a random experiment; each outcome is a sample point. An event is a subset of the sample space — one or more of those outcomes — and is denoted by a capital letter (e.g. A, B).
Sample Space & Events→ Axioms of Probability→ Addition & Multiplication Rules→ Conditional Probability & Bayes' Rule→ Counting Techniques

Once a random phenomenon can be described by a probability, the next natural question is "what values can it take, and how likely is each one?" — that is the subject of random variables and probability distributions, which follows immediately after this topic.
Where every probability problem starts

Before you can calculate a single probability, you need precise vocabulary for describing a chance process: what counts as an experiment, what its possible outcomes are, and how we define and count the events built from those outcomes.
Experiment, trial, outcome

Experiment Any process that generates a set of data or well-defined outcomes. There are two types: deterministic experiments, where the observed result is not subject to chance, and random (chance) experiments, whose outcome cannot be predicted with certainty — as simple as tossing a coin or die, or as complex as testing 50 people from a population for a disease.

Trial
Each repetition of an experiment is called a trial — a single performance of the experiment.

Outcome The possible result of a single trial of an experiment. Outcomes are equally likely when each one has the same chance of occurring as the others. Example: tossing a coin gives outcomes {H, T}; rolling a die gives {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}; a football match gives {win (W), loss (L), draw (D)}.
Constructing sample spaces
Two tosses of a coin
S = {HH, HT, TH, TT} — 4 equally likely outcomes.
Three tosses of a coin
S = {HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT} — 8 equally likely outcomes.
Sex of three children
Each child equally likely B or G: S = {BBB, BBG, BGB, BGG, GBB, GBG, GGB, GGG} — 8 outcomes (analogous to 3 coin tosses).
Rolling two dice
Each die shows 1–6, so S consists of all ordered pairs (i, j) with i, j ∈ {1,…,6} — 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes, from (1,1) to (6,6).
Events: simple and compound

Event An event is a collection of one or more outcomes from an experiment — a subset of the sample space, denoted by a capital letter. Example: the event of observing exactly one head in three tosses of a coin is A = {HTT, THT, TTH}. For a couple planning three children, the event of having exactly two girls is D = {BGG, GBG, GGB}.

Simple vs. compound event An event with exactly one outcome is a simple event (e.g. rolling a single 6 on a die). An event with two or more outcomes is a compound event — e.g. rolling an odd number on a die is compound, since it consists of the three outcomes {1, 3, 5}.

Tree diagram
A tree diagram pictures the outcomes of a random experiment as branching paths. The probability of an outcome that is a sequence of trials (e.g. the sex of three successive children) is represented by following one path of the tree from start to end.
Probability of an event, P(A)

P(A) — the probability of event A A numerical measure of the likelihood that event A occurs, such that 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1. If P(A) = 0, event A is impossible; if P(A) = 1, A is certain. If A′ is the complement of A (A does not occur), then P(A′) = 1 − P(A).
There are three schools of thought for defining/interpreting P(A): the Classical Definition and the Empirical Concept (together the "Objective Approach"), and the Subjective Approach.
Classical definition

Assumes all outcomes are equally likely. If an experiment has n mutually exclusive, equally likely outcomes: P(A) = n(A)/n(S) = (number of successful outcomes)/(number of possible outcomes). Called priori probability because it's fixed before the experiment is even run.
Empirical concept

P(A) = (number of times A occurred in the past) / (total number of observations) — a relative frequency, which becomes more accurate as trials are repeated. Called posterior probability since it's found only after event A has been observed (e.g. rolling a die 6000 times and tallying results).
Subjective approach

Based on degree of belief through available evidence — assessed through experience, intuition, judgement or expertise (e.g. "the probability this patient's condition will be cured"). This is the more recently developed approach and underlies Bayesian Decision Analysis.
A couple is planning to have three children, and each child born is equally likely to be a boy (B) or a girl (G). (a) List the sample space. (b) Find the probability the couple has exactly two girls.

items: 1Write out the sample space of all 2³ = 8 equally-likely birth orders.S = {BBB, BBG, BGB, BGG, GBB, GBG, GGB, GGG} — 8 outcomes total
2Let A = the event of exactly two girls, and list its outcomes.A = {BGG, GBG, GGB} → n(A) = 3
3Apply the classical definition, P(A) = n(A)/n(S).P(A) = 3/8 = 0.375

blocks.x: Answer: P(exactly two girls) = 3/8 = 0.375.

blocks.title: Quick self-check: simple or compound event?

items: "The die shows a 4" → simple event (one outcome).
"The die shows an even number" → compound event ({2, 4, 6}, three outcomes).
"Exactly two of three children are girls" → compound event (three outcomes: BGG, GBG, GGB).
A coin lands heads on a single toss → simple event.

blocks.x: The rules every probability must obey

To keep probability assignments consistent with intuition, every valid assignment of P(A) must satisfy a short list of axioms. From those axioms, the addition rule and multiplication law follow — the two workhorse tools for computing the probability of combined ("compound") events.
Axioms of probability (Kolmogorov's axioms)
Given an experiment and a sample space S, the objective of probability is to assign to each event A a number P(A) that precisely measures the chance A will occur. All such assignments must satisfy:
A.1 For every event A, 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1.
A.2 P(S) = 1 — the probability of the entire sample space (something in S happening) is certainty.
A.3 If A and B are mutually exclusive events (A ∩ B = ∅), then P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B).
A.4 If A₁, A₂, …, Aₙ is a sequence of n mutually exclusive events, then P(A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ … ∪ Aₙ) = P(A₁) + P(A₂) + … + P(Aₙ) — the general n-event extension of A.3.
Mutually exclusive & exhaustive events

Mutually exclusive events Two or more events with no common outcomes (they never occur at the same time). If A and B are mutually exclusive, A ∩ B = ∅ and so P(A ∩ B) = 0, which is why P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) for such events.

Exhaustive events & partitions Events defined on the same sample space are exhaustive if their union equals S. A collection A₁, A₂, …, Aₙ forms a partition of S if (a) each Aᵢ ≠ ∅, (b) Aᵢ ∩ Aⱼ = ∅ for all i ≠ j (mutually exclusive), and (c) A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ … ∪ Aₙ = S (collectively exhaustive). Partitions are the key idea behind the Total Probability Rule covered in the next tab.
The addition rule
General case — the event (A ∪ B) For any two events A and B: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). The event (A ∪ B) occurs if A or B (or both) occur; the event (A ∩ B) occurs if both A and B occur.

Three-event general case
P(A₁∪A₂∪A₃) = P(A₁)+P(A₂)+P(A₃) − P(A₁∩A₂) − P(A₁∩A₃) − P(A₂∩A₃) + P(A₁∩A₂∩A₃).
Mutually exclusive events (special case) If A₁, A₂, …, Aₙ are mutually exclusive, the overlap terms vanish and the rule simplifies to P(A₁∪A₂∪…∪Aₙ) = P(A₁)+P(A₂)+…+P(Aₙ) — this is just Axiom A.4.

In a population of women, 40% have had breast cancer, 20% are smokers, and 13% are smokers and have had breast cancer. If a woman is selected at random, what is the probability she had breast cancer, smokes, or both?

items: 1Define events and record the given probabilities.B = breast cancer, W = smoker. P(B) = 0.40, P(W) = 0.20, P(B ∩ W) = 0.13
2Apply the general addition rule (these events are not mutually exclusive, since they overlap).P(B ∪ W) = P(B) + P(W) − P(B ∩ W)
3Substitute and compute.P(B ∪ W) = 0.40 + 0.20 − 0.13 = 0.47

blocks.x: Answer: P(breast cancer or smoker or both) = 0.47.
The multiplication law of probability
Multiplying both sides of the conditional-probability definition P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) by P(B) gives the multiplication rule, which lets us calculate the probability that two events both occur.

Multiplication rule (two events) If events A and B can both occur, P(A ∩ B) = P(B)P(A|B) = P(A)P(B|A). Since A∩B and B∩A are equivalent, it does not matter which event is labelled A and which is labelled B.
Multiplication rule extended to three or more events For three events: P(A∩B∩C) = P(A)·P(B|A)·P(C|A∩B). By induction, for n events: P(A₁∩A₂∩…∩Aₙ) = P(A₁)·P(A₂|A₁)·P(A₃|A₁∩A₂)…P(Aₙ|A₁∩A₂∩…∩Aₙ₋₁).
A clinic has 20 patients, of whom 5 have hypertension. If 2 patients are selected at random in succession, without replacing the first, what is the probability both patients have hypertension?

items: 1Define A = first patient has hypertension, B = second patient has hypertension. We want P(A ∩ B).P(A) = 5/20
2Given A has occurred, only 4 hypertensive patients remain among the 19 left.P(B|A) = 4/19
3Apply the multiplication rule, P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B|A).P(A∩B) = (5/20)(4/19) = 20/380 = 1/19

blocks.x: Answer: P(both have hypertension) = 1/19 ≈ 0.0526.

blocks.title: Addition rule vs. multiplication rule — when to use which?

items: Use the addition rule when you need P(A or B) — the union.
Use the multiplication rule when you need P(A and B) — the intersection.
For mutually exclusive events, the addition rule simplifies (no overlap to subtract); for independent events (next tab), the multiplication rule simplifies to P(A)P(B), with no conditioning needed.

blocks.x: Updating probability with new information

Most real probability questions are really "given what I now know, how likely is this?" Conditional probability formalises that update, independence tells us when new information changes nothing, and Bayes' Rule lets us flip a conditional probability around — the exact logic behind interpreting a diagnostic test result.
Conditional probability

P(A|B) — probability of A given B Let A and B be events in sample space S with P(B) > 0. The probability that A occurs given that B has already occurred is P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B). If P(B) = 0, P(A|B) is undefined. In a finite equiprobable space, P(A∩B) = n(A∩B)/n(S) and P(B) = n(B)/n(S).

Conditional probability satisfies the probability axioms
When P(B) > 0: (1) P(A|B) ≥ 0; (2) P(B|B) = 1; (3) for pairwise mutually exclusive events A₁, A₂, …, P(∪Aᵢ | B) = ΣP(Aᵢ|B) — i.e. P(·|B) behaves exactly like an ordinary probability function.

In a population, 8% have sickle cell trait, 30% of those with sickle cell trait also have a family history of sickle cell disease, and 5% have a family history of sickle cell disease. An individual is selected at random. (a) Find the probability the individual has both sickle cell trait and a family history. (b) Given the individual has a family history, find the probability they have sickle cell trait.

items: 1Define S = has sickle cell trait, F = has family history. Record the given information.P(S) = 0.08, P(F|S) = 0.30, P(F) = 0.05
2(a) Use the multiplication rule: P(S ∩ F) = P(F|S)·P(S).P(S ∩ F) = (0.30)(0.08) = 0.024
3(b) Use the conditional probability formula: P(S|F) = P(S∩F)/P(F).P(S|F) = 0.024 / 0.05 = 0.48

blocks.x: Independent events

Independence Events A and B (nonzero probabilities) are independent if and only if any one of these equivalent statements holds: P(A|B) = P(A); P(B|A) = P(B); or P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B). Otherwise A and B are dependent. (Note: if A and B are such that P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B|A) but the simple product rule fails, they are said to be only conditionally independent.)

Why the conditions are equivalent
If A and B are independent, then P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) = P(A)P(B)/P(B) = P(A), and symmetrically P(B|A) = P(A)P(B)/P(A) = P(B) — knowing one event occurred changes nothing about the probability of the other.

A patient is tested for two unrelated conditions: vitamin D deficiency (P(V) = 0.35) and anemia (P(A) = 0.20), assumed independent. Find: (a) P(both conditions); (b) P(at least one condition); (c) P(neither condition).

items: 1(a) Independent events: P(V ∩ A) = P(V)·P(A).P(V ∩ A) = (0.35)(0.20) = 0.07
2(b) Apply the addition rule for P(V ∪ A).P(V ∪ A) = 0.35 + 0.20 − 0.07 = 0.48
3(c) "Neither" is the complement of "at least one"; also check via independence of the complements.P(V̄ ∩ Ā) = 1 − 0.48 = 0.52 (or: (0.65)(0.80) = 0.52)

blocks.x: The Total Probability Rule (Law of Total Probability)

Total probability rule If A₁, A₂, …, Aₙ form a partition of S, then for any event B on S with P(B) > 0: P(B) = Σᵢ P(Aᵢ)·P(B|Aᵢ). In the simplest case, since A and Ā partition S, A = (A∩B) ∪ (A∩B̄), so P(A) = P(A|B)P(B) + P(A|B̄)P(B̄). This is useful because P(A|B), P(A|B̄) and P(B) are often easy to obtain from context, even when P(A) directly is not.

A hospital classifies surgical patients as "high-risk" or "low-risk" for post-operative infection. P(infection | high-risk) = 0.4, P(infection | low-risk) = 0.2, and 30% of the patient population is high-risk. (a) Find the overall probability a randomly selected patient develops an infection. (b) If a patient develops an infection, find the probability they were high-risk.

items: 1Define I = develops infection, H = high-risk. Record the given data.P(H) = 0.3, P(I|H) = 0.4, P(H̄) = 0.7, P(I|H̄) = 0.2
2(a) Apply the total probability rule.P(I) = (0.4)(0.3) + (0.2)(0.7) = 0.12 + 0.14 = 0.26
3(b) Apply Bayes' Rule: P(H|I) = P(I|H)P(H)/P(I).P(H|I) = 0.12 / 0.26 = 6/13 ≈ 0.46

blocks.x: Bayes' Rule

Bayes' Rule Let A and Aᶜ partition S with P(A) > 0, P(Aᶜ) > 0. For any event B with P(B) > 0: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A) / [P(B|A)P(A) + P(B|Aᶜ)P(Aᶜ)]. It follows from the definitions of conditional probability and the total probability rule, and lets us "invert" a conditional probability we know (e.g. P(test result | disease)) to find the one we actually want (P(disease | test result)).

A screening test is 95% effective at detecting a disease when present (sensitivity) and, when the disease is absent, is 99% effective at declaring the subject negative (specificity). 8% of the population has the disease (prevalence). Given a positive test result, what is the probability the subject actually has the disease?

items: 1Define D = disease present, A = test positive. Record the data.P(D) = 0.08, P(A|D) = 0.95 (sensitivity), P(Ā|D̄) = 0.99 (specificity) → P(A|D̄) = 0.01
3Compute numerator, denominator, then divide.= 0.076 / (0.076 + 0.0092) = 0.076 / 0.0852 ≈ 0.892

blocks.x: Answer: P(disease | positive test) ≈ 0.892. (A symmetric calculation gives P(disease | negative test) = (0.05)(0.08) / [(0.05)(0.08)+(0.99)(0.92)] ≈ 0.004 — a negative result is very reassuring here.)
Sensitivity, specificity & the 2×2 classification table

Define D = disease present, D̄ = disease absent, T = positive test, T̄ = negative test. Cross-classifying n subjects by disease status and test result gives the table below (a, b, c, d are cell counts).
Sensitivity
P(T|D) — the probability of a positive test result given the disease is present.
Specificity
P(T̄|D̄) — the probability of a negative test result given the disease is absent.
False positive
P(T|D̄) — test says positive, but the disease is actually absent.
False negative
P(T̄|D) — test says negative, but the disease is actually present.

blocks.title: Independence vs. conditional probability — don't mix them up

items: If A and B are independent, P(A|B) simply equals P(A) — conditioning on B tells you nothing new.
If A and B are dependent, P(A|B) ≠ P(A) in general — this is exactly the situation Bayes' Rule and the Total Probability Rule are built to handle.
A high sensitivity test can still have a low P(D|T) (positive predictive value) if the disease is rare — this is the core lesson of the Bayes' Rule worked example above.

blocks.x: Counting before you calculate

The classical definition of probability, P(A) = n(A)/n(S), requires you to count outcomes — and for anything beyond a coin or a die, listing every outcome by hand quickly becomes impossible. Permutations and combinations are the two systematic counting tools that make this practical.
Permutations

Permutation A permutation is an ordered arrangement of objects — it tells us how many possible orderings there can be for a given set of objects. If all objects are distinct, in a permutation they cannot be repeated.
n distinct objects, taken all together n! = n(n − 1)(n − 2)…3·2·1 — the number of ways to arrange all n distinct objects in order.
n distinct objects, taken k at a time nPk = P(n, k) = n! / (n − k)!, for k < n — the number of ordered arrangements of only k of the n objects.
All 3 letters A, B, C
3! = 6 arrangements: ABC, BAC, ACB, BCA, CAB, CBA.
10 digits, taken 2 at a time
Repeated objects & circular arrangements

Permutations with groups of alike objects If n objects consist of groups where n₁ of the first kind are alike, n₂ of the second kind are alike, …, nₖ of the kth kind are alike (n = n₁+n₂+…+nₖ), the number of distinct arrangements is n! / (n₁!·n₂!·…·nₖ!).

Circular permutations The number of ways to arrange n distinct objects in a circle is n!/n = (n − 1)! — one fewer factorial term than for a straight line, because rotating the whole circle doesn't create a new arrangement.
Find the number of distinct arrangements of the letters of the 14-letter word SCIENTIFICALLY, which contains 2 C's, 3 I's, 2 L's, and the rest of the letters distinct.

items: 1Identify n and the repeated-letter counts.n = 14, repeats: 2 C's, 3 I's, 2 L's
2Apply the formula for permutations with repeated groups.14! / (2! · 3! · 2!)

blocks.x: Answer: 3,632,428,800 distinct arrangements.
In how many ways can 6 persons be seated around a circular table?

items: 1This is a circular permutation of n = 6 distinct people.(n − 1)! = (6 − 1)!

blocks.x: Answer: 120 distinct circular seating arrangements.
Combinations

Combination A combination is an arrangement of objects with no respect to order — combinations are basically "selections." The number of ways to select k objects from n distinct objects, irrespective of order, is:
nCk or (ⁿₖ) nCk = n! / [(n − k)! · k!] = nPk / k! — a combination is a permutation with the k! orderings of the chosen objects divided back out, since order no longer matters.
From a group of 5 surgeons, you must select 3 to join you in performing a specialised surgery. In how many different ways can you select the three surgeons?

items: 1Order of selection doesn't matter here, so use combinations with n = 5, k = 3.<sup>5</sup>C₃ = 5! / [3!(5 − 3)!]
3Divide to find the answer.= 10

blocks.x: Answer: 10 different ways to select the three surgeons.
Counting techniques inside a probability calculation

Permutations and combinations become most powerful when combined with the classical definition P(A) = n(A)/n(S): count the "successful" arrangements/selections, count the total possible ones, and divide.
A hospital committee of 4 is chosen at random from a pool of 6 male and 5 female staff (11 people total). What is the probability the committee has exactly 2 men and 2 women?

items: 1Count the total number of possible committees of 4 from 11 people (order doesn't matter → combination).n(S) = <sup>11</sup>C₄ = 11!/(4!7!) = (11×10×9×8)/(4×3×2×1) = 7920/24 = 330
2Count the favourable outcomes: choose 2 of the 6 men AND 2 of the 5 women, then multiply (multiplication principle for independent choices).<sup>6</sup>C₂ × <sup>5</sup>C₂ = 15 × 10 = 150
3Apply the classical definition of probability, P(A) = n(A)/n(S).P(exactly 2 men & 2 women) = 150/330 = 5/11 ≈ 0.4545

blocks.x: Answer: P(exactly 2 men and 2 women) = 5/11 ≈ 0.4545.

blocks.title: Permutation or combination — how to tell them apart

items: Ask: does order matter? Arranging patients in a queue, assigning medal positions (1st/2nd/3rd), or forming a PIN → order matters → permutation.
Choosing a committee, a surgical team, or a hand of cards where only the set selected matters → order doesn't matter → combination.
Numerically, <sup>n</sup>C<sub>k</sub> is always <sup>n</sup>P<sub>k</sub> divided by k! — combinations "collapse" all k! orderings of the same selection into a single count.
Once you can count n(A) and n(S) this way, you can plug straight into the classical probability formula P(A) = n(A)/n(S) — exactly as in the committee example above.
